blogs.title: When Penalties Belong to the State: The Eighth Circuit’s Interpretation of Minnesota’s Wage Penalty Schemes
blogs.description: This post dissects the court’s analysis of the Minnesota Payment of Wages Act and the Minnesota Wage Theft Act, focusing on why the court concluded that only the Commissioner—not an employee—may seek average‑daily‑wage penalties. It evaluates the statutory construction, the legislative history showing the legislature’s ability to grant penalties directly to workers, and the broader implications for wage‑and‑hour plaintiffs across the Midwest who may have relied on civil penalties as a leverage tool.

blogs.title: Standing, Mootness, and Civil Penalties: Why the MFLSA Claim Was Sent Back for a Jurisdictional Ruling
blogs.description: This article explores the Ninth Circuit’s (actually Eighth Circuit) handling of the plaintiff’s claim for statutory penalties under the Minnesota Fair Labor Standards Act. It breaks down the standing and mootness analysis, compares the MFLSA penalty regime to the Supreme Court’s Friends of the Earth framework, and discusses how the vacatur and remand create a roadmap for future cases where employers have already remedied wage back‑pay but may continue unlawful policies.

blogs.title: The Perils of Stipulating “All Claims Resolved” Before Summary Judgment: Lessons from Cohen v. Consilio
blogs.description: A deep dive into the strategic use of stipulations in wage‑and‑hour litigation. The post examines how the parties’ agreement that Cohen had been paid all overtime wages and liquidated damages shaped the district court’s summary‑judgment analysis, yet left open the question of penalties and injunctive relief. It offers practical guidance for litigators on drafting and negotiating stipulations to avoid unintended remands.

blogs.title: Injunctions in Wage‑and‑Hour Disputes: Why the Eighth Circuit Refused to Grant Relief in Cohen’s Case
blogs.description: This piece analyzes the procedural hurdles that barred the court from entertaining Cohen’s request for an injunction rescinding the “illegal” overtime policy. It discusses the timing of claim amendments, the standards for injunctive relief in employment law, and what plaintiffs must do to preserve injunctive claims when the case pivots to statutory penalties or damages.
